title: δεν, μην, questions and question words
goal: Negate any verb correctly and ask yes/no and wh- questions.

blocks.text: Greek questions need no inversion and no auxiliary: intonation alone turns a statement into a question, and the question mark is written **;**. Negation has two words, and choosing between them is a matter of mood: **δεν** with the indicative (statements, θα-futures), **μην** with the subjunctive (after να, ας) and in prohibitions.

blocks.title: Yes/no and wh- questions
items: Intonation only marks a yes/no question: Έχεις νέα; 'Do you have news?'
μήπως softens or hedges: Μήπως ξέρεις...; 'Do you happen to know...?'
A preposition stays in front of its question word, never at the end: Με ποιον μίλησες; 'Who did you talk to?'

blocks.title: δεν or μην?
items: **δεν** + indicative: Δεν ξέρω. Δεν θα έρθει (δεν stands before θα).
**μην** after να or ας: Να μην αργήσεις. Ας μην πάμε.
**μην** in prohibitions, with or without να: Μην το αγγίζεις! (Να) μη φύγεις!
**μη(ν)**: the ν is kept before a vowel and κ, π, τ, γκ, μπ, ντ, ξ, ψ, like τη(ν).
Standing alone, 'no' to a suggestion is όχι; an answer to a negative question uses ναι/όχι as in English.

blocks.title: Ναι, όχι and the head toss
blocks.text: Two traps for English speakers. **Ναι** 'yes' sounds like *nay*, and **όχι** 'no' has no n in it. Then there is the body language: a quick upward toss of the head, often with raised eyebrows and a click of the tongue, means **όχι**, and can look like a nod to foreigners. 'Yes' is a small downward nod, often tilted. Colloquial no's include **μπα** 'nah' and the flat **Όχι, ρε!** In formal answers you hear **μάλιστα** 'yes, certainly'. Negative words need δεν as well: **Δεν ξέρω τίποτα** 'I know nothing', **Δεν ήρθε κανείς** 'Nobody came'.

items.why: Indicative statement: δεν.
After να: μην.
A prohibition takes μην.
δεν stands before θα.
Asking about place: accented πού.
πόσο as an adverb: how much?
After a preposition the accusative: ποιον.
γιατί asks 'why' and answers 'because'.
After ας: μην.

items.prompt: How do you say 'I never drink coffee'?
items.why: ποτέ 'never' still needs δεν with the verb (negative concord).
μήπως makes a polite, hedged question.
ποιος declines like an adjective and agrees with its noun: το βιβλίο → ποιο.

items.prompt: ___ είναι η Μαρία; Η αδερφή μου.
items.why: Feminine subject: ποια.
Unaccented πως means 'that'; πώς asks 'how?'.
Standing alone, 'no' is όχι; δεν and μην only go with a verb.
After να the negative is μην, placed between να and the verb.
Negative concord: δεν + κανείς 'nobody'.
With δεν, 'anything / nothing' is τίποτα.
The idiom uses the genitive plural: πόσων χρονών.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *I'm not coming tomorrow.*
items.why: Indicative (present or θα-future): δεν, which stands before θα.

items.prompt: Say in Greek to a friend: *Don't leave!*
items.why: A prohibition takes μη(ν), with or without να.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *Where is the station?*
items.why: Accented πού asks about place; no inversion needed.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *When does the train leave?*
items.why: πότε 'when?', stressed on the first syllable.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *How much does it cost?*
items.why: Adverb πόσο; Πόσο κάνει; is the everyday shop version.

items.prompt: Say in Greek to a friend: *Who are you talking to?*
items.why: The preposition stays in front of the question word, which goes into the accusative.

items.prompt: Say in Greek to a friend: *Why aren't you eating?* (τρως)
items.why: γιατί 'why?' + δεν + indicative.
After να: μην.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *Do you happen to have a pen?* (μήπως, στυλό)
items.why: μήπως softens a question into 'by any chance'.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *We never go there.* (εκεί)
items.why: ποτέ 'never' still needs δεν with the verb.
Polite plural θέλετε; τι 'what?' never declines.
After ας: μη(ν); before μ the ν is usually dropped.
